articles.text: Interested residents may apply until May 5 The city of Piedmont is seeking volunteers to serve on the newly established Community Pool Advisory Committee (PAC). Residents have until Wednesday, May 5 to apply. Committee members will offer advice throughout the design process, as well as serve as a conduit for the community’s needs in the design refinement and construction of the pool. The committee will not be responsible for managing or directing project activities; instead, the committee is expected to use the experience and expertise of its members to provide support and insight to staff and city council members for the $19 million project. Main responsibilities of PAC members will include: ensuring the project meets community expectations, communicating project progress to residents, and making recommendations to staff on how to best balance any conflicting priorities with budget resources and community expectations. The PAC will consist of five to seven residents. Recruitment for the committee takes place separately from recruitment that has taken place for other commissions and committees. City staff will announce the recruitment period on the city website and social media channels, as well as with a press release. After receiving applications from interested residents, city council will then conduct interviews of qualified candidates. The council will appoint a Chair of the committee and its members. Interested residents may download the “Application for Appointive Vacancy” from the city’s website and apply online at https:// piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Editor: I was saddened to read Shirley Hooi’s letter more or less admonishing PUSD to stay in their lane as it concerns race relations and history including current events. I would suggest that her letter is exactly the reason the schools need to talk about race. Her most memorable anecdotal stories from her childhood 35 years ago were being asked if she spoke English by PPD and being jumped by two black youth. Using a modern lens, I would say the African American youth from her attack should be considered “a one off, a bad apple; the whole barrel isn’t rotten, just a few bad seeds.” We have extended that identical courtesy to every single officer involved in shootings of unarmed black people. Until [recently], most police officers involved in murdering unarmed black folks have kept both their pension and freedom. I want to scream for every mother, myself included, who wonders if today is the day some jumpy cop is going to kill my son. Is today the day that some racist neighbor is going to murder my son for wearing a hoodie? Is today the day my son will be executed by white men for running in the wrong neighborhood? Will my other son be lynched for looking at a white woman? The three black men in this household have multiple negative anecdotal stories because they have had the audacity to drive, bike, walk, ride the elevator, and shop in a department store all the while being black men. My husband went to a tworoom, segregated school specifically for “coloreds” 10 years after Brown v. Board of Education. The subhuman and racist treatment of people of color, specifically black men, in my immediate family spans decades. If Ms. Hooi’s letter is any indication, even some educated parents in this town aren’t talking about race with their kids other than to shut down uncomfortable conversation with terse responses. It would seem counter intuitive, given Ms. Hooi’s selfproclaimed blunt answers to her children, that she would have an in-depth conversation about race being that she herself trotted out a rather tone-deaf response. It’s not enough in 2021 to “not be a racist” The easiest way to obliterate white guilt is to be an ally to people of color. You cannot be an ally if you don’t listen, if you don’t acknowledge and if you don’t converse. Please keep race relations, current and historic in this country as part of the PUSD curriculum. To do otherwise is a tragedy we cannot afford to repeat. –Sydney Proctor
articles.title: Becoming an ally by listening

articles.text: “I am a voice crying in the wilderness, Make the Lord’s path straight.” John the Baptist stood proudly in the tradition of the biblical prophets. He stood in the tradition of Moses who led the people to freedom and toward an understanding of what it meant to be the people of God. He stood in the tradition of Elijah who knew what it was like to face hostility, to feel alone and afraid, even as God’s words poured from his mouth. He stood in the tradition of Jeremiah who strove to counter the self-serving lies of the religious and political establishments. Consider John’s use of the words voice, cry and wilderness. Like John himself, these are words that are central to the biblical story. It is God’s voice that calls forth the created order. It is God’s voice that calls Abraham to journey to a distant land. It is God’s voice that calls the exiles home from Babylon. When the people are enslaved in Egypt, they cry out in pain, they cry out for liberation. God hears their cry. God is moved by their cry. When Job’s friends insult him rather than encourage him, he cries to God for a hearing, a face-to-face meeting. God responds to Job’s cry. When the people cry out from exile “how can we sing God’s song in this strange and foreign land?”, God acts to bring them home. When there is crying, God is near. After the people are liberated from Egypt, God leads them into the wilderness. In the wilderness God instructs them. In the wilderness God provides for them. In the wilderness they come to understand that God will never leave them or forsake them. Voice. Cry. Wilderness. Biblical words. John’s words. Important words. Human experience words. We live in a time in which we have many opportunities to opt in and/or to opt out. We can opt in or opt out of service contracts when purchasing a phone, opt in or opt out of protections in regard to how our personal information is shared, opt in or opt out of participating in the political process, opt in or opt out of belonging to a faith community. Voice. Cry. Wilderness. With these words John makes it clear
articles.title: God chooses to opt-in to the human story

articles.text: The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD), will hold a public hearing on proposed rate increases to water and wastewater service charges. The virtual meeting will be held on Tuesday, June 8 at 1:15 p.m. A notice was mailed to customers in Alameda, Albany, Berkeley, El Cerrito, Emeryville, Kensington, Oakland, and Piedmont last week. EBMUD is proposing to increase the rates for both its water and wastewater service charges based on its most recent rate models and cost of service studies. Rates would increase over a two-year period, by approximately 4 percent overall on July 1, 2021, followed by another 4 percent increase the next year, July 1, 2022. This is an approximate increase. Individual bills may increase by slightly more or less that amount depending on the specific rates and charges that apply to you and how much water you use. The notice mailed to residents provides an example of an average single family residence which could expect a water rate increase of $5.19 per month, and a wastewater increase of $1.87 per month. A temporary “Drought Surcharge” may be assessed on all potable water use during a declared drought or water shortage. EBMUD has not yet declared a drought. Drought surcharges are calculated to recover costs of providing supplemental water, cost of water-shortage related customer service, and losses of revenue. How to participate in the hearing The board of directors will hold the public hearing on June 8, which will be conducted via Zoom. The public may participate in the hearing virtual or by telephone. The Zoom Meeting ID is 958-6681-4531, and the passcode is 810650. You must enter both numbers to participate in the meeting telephonically (by calling 1-699-900-6833) or virtually (by visiting www.edmud.com/ rates.) Written comments may be mailed before the hearing date to EBMUD, MS 218, PO Box 24055, Oakland, CA 94623-1055. The first event focused on the City’s Climate Action Plan, a document approved by Council that sets emissions goals for the City. Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman and Americorps Fellow Nate Redinbo led participants through a brief overview of the Plan and highlighted actions staff had taken over the last 12 months to meet the CAP goals. Highlights included the February passage of energy reach codes through council, and a continued focus on transportation and solid waste management. Staff then asked participants to offer suggestions and thoughts on actions to take next. In the evening, staff held a panel discussion with new Fire Chief David Brannigan, Fire Captain Scott Barringer, and wildland fire scientist Dr. Sasha Berleman on the film Rebuilding Paradise and Piedmont’s fire management practices. Audience members asked questions ranging from the fire safety of various native species to evacuation plans. Dr. Berleman described controlled burns and the future of firefighting measures. Piedmont firefighters highlighted steps residents can take to be fire safe. At the conclusion of the presentation, City staff announced the winners of the Piedmont Climate Challenge and the grand prize – a community native tree to be planted in a public location. articles.text: On Tuesday, April 27, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention updated its guidance on masking, announcing that people fully vaccinated against the COVID-19 virus do not need to wear masks outdoors unless they are in a crowd of strangers. Soon after the CDC announcement, California Governor Gavin Newsom said that he would update California’s mask mandate to match the new guidance. “After reviewing the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s masking recommendations, and with science and data as our guide, we are moving to align California’s guidance with these common-sense updates,” Newsom said in a statement. People are considered fully vaccinated if it has been two weeks since either their second dose of Pfizer or Moderna vaccine or their one dose of Johnson & Johnson vaccine. The CDC said that fully vaccinated people can participate in most outdoor activities, like small outdoor gatherings or outdoor dining, without a mask. However, masks are recommended in crowded outdoor settings and venues, like packed stadiums and large concerts. “We will continue to recommend this until widespread vaccination is achieved,” CDC Director Dr. Rochelle Walensky said in a White House briefing yesterday. The number of new COVID- 19 cases has remained low in California, Alameda County and Piedmont this week, with California now having some of the lowest positivity rates in the nation. No new cases of COVID- 19 have been reported in Piedmont across the past seven days, according to Alameda County Public Health Department data. The total number of Piedmont cases since the pandemic began is 176. The positivity rate for the county is 1.4 percent as of Monday, April 26, a slight decrease from last week. The positivity rate has not been above 2 percent since February 25. Across Alameda County, the total caseload is 85,683 – an increase of only 215 new cases week-over-week, a large decrease compared to recent weeks. There have been 26,664 cases recorded in Oakland and 13,333 cases in Hayward. Tragically, another 14 people have died of COVID-19 in Alameda County, bringing the total number of fatalities countywide to 1,491. In terms of reopening businesses and activities, Alameda County moved into the orange tier on March 30. The orange tier, or moderate tier, is the second-least restrictive tier in California’s color-coded four-tier reopening protocol. The county has met orange tier metrics for several weeks but has not yet met benchmarks to move into the least-restrictive yellow tier, or minimal tier. To move up into the yellow tier, the positivity rate needs to stay below 2 percent. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 1 – right now there are 3.6 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to stay below 2.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. Only four of California’s 58 counties are in the yellow tier. All Bay Area counties are in the orange tier besides Solano County, which is in the more-restrictive red tier. If San Francisco and Marin counties continue to meet yellow tier metrics, they could move into the least-restrictive tier next week. In the yellow tier, most indoor operations are allowed with modifications.

articles.text: PHS senior Jake Ochoa He’s not yet old enough to get one on his body, but 17-year-old Jake Ochoa has tattoos on his mind. For this visual artist, it’s mainly about the self-expression that tattoos represent. “I saw a YouTube video about tattoos, and this tattoo artist said, basically, that we don’t get to choose the body that we’re born with, but we can choose how we decorate it,” said the Piedmont High School student. “That really resonated with me. It’s decorating in the purest sense.” Ochoa’s interest in tattoos started three years ago when he was a freshman. He is now concentrating on tattoo imagery and culture for his Advanced Placement Art class project. “There are a lot of different styles,” he said. “[Tattooing]’s a window into different cultures, different lifestyles.” A fan of the uniformity of traditional Japanese tattoos, Ochoa also appreciates the unorthodox art of Neo-traditional tattoos. “I’m really getting into Polynesian and Filipino tattoos,” he said. “The imagery is always fascinating. There’s a flow; they fit onto the body really well. I find that composition really appealing.” Ochoa will display his tattoo-influenced designs on small paper items, like prints or bookmarks, at this year’s Piedmont Art Walk. But some day, with a lot of training and financial security, he might start inking his designs onto the skin of paying customers. “There’s a lot of merit to doing it; it’s creatively stimulating,” “8Dragon” by Jake Ochoa he said. “It’s stressful, because you’re marking someone’s skin. But I think it’d be a fun adventure. Tattooing is something I’d like to do in the future – when I have free time, and when I’m old enough to get the machines.” Ochoa plans to study graphic design at college next year.

articles.text: I spent a few hours last week talking to a mom who was wracked with guilt. The problem was her son, she explained, who was struggling in school. His grades had dropped in a few classes and she was beside herself with self-recrimination. I should have done this, she said. Or that. Or maybe I should have done something completely different. It took me a while to follow her logic, but it went something like this: if she had just known more, done more, and helped more, then her child wouldn’t be suffering. This is a trap many parents fall into these days, especially in the midst of COVID. You believe that it is your job to prevent your child’s suffering, and because so many kids are suffering in COVID, it means you’re doing a terrible job, or even worse, that you’ve failed as parents. The mom I spoke with certainly believed this, and it was making her life miserable. Parents: raise your hands if, at some point during this disastrous year, you have worried that you aren’t doing enough for your kids. I’m assuming that’s all of you, so I have a few words of advice. The best thing you can do for Forgiveness leads to healing. your kids right now is to forgive yourself, unconditionally, for every misstep you’ve made this year, no matter how big. And I mean it: forgive yourself for everything. Here’s why: your concern about your own shortcomings weighs you down, and it leaves you less able to attend to all of the important things in your life, such as your child’s suffering. Because while it’s futile to focus on preventing suffering – something that is impossible – it is helpful to focus on soothing the suffering, which is quite a different matter. You can begin this process by soothing yourself, forgiving yourself, having a good cry, and recognizing that this has been a horrible year. Forget about silver linings for the moment. Focus on being tender and kind to yourself, in your role as a parent, and recognize that the best next step is to forgive your child too. It’s been an awful time, and it’s not over yet, but we can ease our pain by not second-guessing, criticizing, or punishing ourselves for not being perfect. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. articles.text: Double Play, the independent robotics team of Eva and Mikey Swei and neighbor Jasper Schuetz, qualified for the 2021 VEX World Championship by receiving the Design Award at the VEX California State Championship in April for their robot designed to put basketballs through hoops. The Swei siblings got their start in robotics by learning about VEX competitions from their older cousins who competed for Head Royce Robotics. Mikey started competing as a 4th grader. As a 5th grader last year, he competed in the VEX High School Division with sister Eva, then a PHS freshman. They recruited Schuetz for more support in building, designing, and programming. VEX has over 200,000 teams from 50 countries competing worldwide. Every year, a new challenge is revealed with aspects of driving, shooting, lifting, stacking and other tasks in a tournament format. At tournaments, teams are required to pair up in alliances and compete with two other teams. In this year’s challenge, Double Play engineered a robot that can pick up and score balls in goals, similar to basketball. Over the course of a year, the team has spent over 400 hours building, designing, and programming the robot. You can watch their robot reveal here:yout ube.com / watch?v=mPFmXM4kCZo or search “8OOO1B Double Play” on Youtube. For more information about VEX and this year’s challenge, see vexrobotics.com/v5/competition

articles.text: Consumer Affairs Reporter PG&E customers in Alameda County recently received a letter informing them that PG&E would be switching them to a time of use (TOU) plan on May 1. The letter is part of a large initiative to switch all customers in Northern and Central California to TOU by March 2022. If your reaction is “What does this mean?”, “How will this affect my bill?”, or simply “Huh”?, you are not alone. Paraphrasing the Bible, “It is easier for a camel to fit through the eye of a needle than for a normal person to comprehend PG&E rates.” PG&E offers two broad types of rate plans – TOU and Tiered. In TOU plans, when you use electricity, it determines the rate you pay, while Tiered is based upon how much you use as the basis for the rate. Tiered plans work a lot like marginal income tax brackets. You start with a low rate, but when you pass certain usage points, you move into higher rates on the excess. If you don’t use a lot of electricity, the Tiered Plan might be best, especially if you want to use electricity during peak hours. The Time of Use Plan to which PG&E is switching customers has only two rates: Peak, which is 4-9 PM every day, and Off-Peak, which is everything else. So, if you use a lot of electricity but are generally able to avoid those peak hours, you could buy most of your electricity at the lower rate. What activities use the most electricity? Electric appliances such as clothes dryers and ovens are examples, but the big energy hogs are air conditioners and electric vehicle recharging. While not a lot of Piedmont residents have air conditioning, many of us do have electric vehicles, which gets very expensive on a Tiered Plan. EV owners almost always do best on a TOU Plan by setting up their charging for off peak hours (we set ours to start at midnight, and it is done by 7 a.m.). And if you do have an air conditioner and need to use it, you would want to cool down your house earlier in the day and turn it off at 4 p.m. to avoid a shock when you view you next bill. So, with these choices – and there are several TOU Plans, including a special one for EVs – how do you choose? PG&E actually provides a pretty neat tool for you: 1. Log on to your account at pge.com 2. Choose “Rate Plans” 3. Choose “Time of Use Rate Plans” 4. Click the orange box marked “Compare Rates” PG&E will show you all of your options, along with your expected annual electric cost based on your most recent twelve months of usage. It will let you switch to any plan you want, but only once a year. As an incentive to get customers to accept the default switch to the new TOU Plan on May 1, PG&E is giving you what amounts to a money back guarantee. If, after a year, you end up paying more on the new plan than you would have under your existing plan, PG&E with refund you the difference. At that point you can continue on the TOU plan or switch to another that makes more sense. So, for most of us, doing nothing and accepting the switch will probably work out fine. However, it’s always a good idea to be an informed consumer, so go online and look at your options. You might find a more cost-effective option for your particular situation. articles.text: Bryan Gardere’s girls’ basketball team burst into their new season on Wednesday, April 21 with a commanding 83-49 victory over Clayton Valley Charter in Concord. Leading 15-9 after the first quarter, they exploded for 29 points in the second quarter to lead 44-20 at halftime. The Highlanders poured in 24 points in the third, 68-38, then added 15 more in the last quarter. Leading all scorers was senior Kai Johnson with 33 points, 14 rebounds, eight steals, and six assists. “Kai does it all. articles.text: Piedmont’s second annual Art Walk will take place this Sunday, May 2, from 12 p.m. to 5 p.m., and will include artworks from more than 40 Piedmont artists. Last year’s event was “born out of necessity,” explained co-organizer Jon Schleuning, when shelter-in-place guidelines had obliterated live events and decimated the arts industry in the process. “Last year, many artists’ open studios were cancelled [due to COVID-19], so artists were looking at a decrease in sales and didn’t have a place to show. The idea was to create a purposely de-centralized art walk that allows artists to showcase and sell their work, with 20 percent of proceeds going to art programs in the schools,” he explained. Schleuning and Larraine Seiden came up with the idea, with help from featured artists Valerie Corvin and Paula Valenzuela, and in May 2020, a group of about 20 Piedmont artists opened their “home studios” for the city’s first organized Art Walk. This year, artist participation has doubled in size. “The Piedmont community believes strongly in the arts, and there’s a real commitment to fostering arts and culture in the schools. It’s one of the benefits of living here,” said Schleuning. “The Art Walk is unique, in that you actually get to see your neighbors’ and community members’ works. It’s wonderful [to discover] that your neighbor may be an amazing photographer or a phenomenal potter.” Similar to last year’s event, artwork will be displayed in front of the artists’ homes and social distancing guidelines will be observed. All featured artists have agreed to guidelines that require a six-foot distance from one another, wearing face coverings, and engaging in no physical contact. Participants also agree to disinfect and wipe down sites as necessary and will make hand sanitizer or other effective disinfectants available. Artwork on display will range from a variety of mediums, including paintings, ceramics, mixed media, sculpture, photography, quilts, and textile art. Piedmont’s long-running Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present Jeff Orlowski’s award-winning documentary, The Social Dilemma, on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The film will be followed by a Question & Answer session with UC Berkeley Law Professor Rebecca Wexler. The film is free by registering at diversityfilmseries.org, and clicking on the “Register for The Social Dilemma button”. The film documents the hidden practices that underlie the business of social media. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. The experts assure us their intentions were good -- even the one whose job title at Facebook was head of “monetization”. Yet all are deeply concerned about what they’ve created, and one confesses that he worked all day on making his site irresistibly seductive and then found himself unable to resist the very algorithmic tricks he helped to create when he went home at night. The most important lesson from the film is that people should question everything they read online, especially if it is presented in a way that reflects a detailed understanding of personal inclinations and preferences. Viewers should learn to resist the “attention extraction model” that makes social media seem friendly and reinforcing. As the New York Times has advised, “Unplug and run”. After viewing The Social Dilemma, join the Diversity Film Series audience for Q & A discussion with Rebecca Wexler, Assistant Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law, and Co-Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology. Wexler teaches, researches, and writes on issues concerning data, technology, and criminal justice. Sign up at www.diversityfilmseries.org for the Diversity Film viewing on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by the City of Piedmont, Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont School District.

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, April 28, 2021 Diversity Film Series to present The Social Dilemma May 13 A still from the documentary, The Social Dilemma. Piedmont’s long-running Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present Jeff Orlowski’s award-winning documentary, The Social Dilemma, on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The film will be followed by a Question & Answer session with UC Berkeley Law Professor Rebecca Wexler. The film is free by registering at diversityfilmseries.org, and clicking on the “Register for The Social Dilemma button”. The film documents the hidden practices that underlie the business of social media. Viewers will learn that the algorithms designed to capture your attention are also profoundly affecting your brains and beliefs in ways that directly threaten democracy. An internal Facebook report by sociologist Monica Lee states, “64% of the people who joined extremist groups on Facebook did so because the algorithms steered them there.” Other documentaries have raised concerns about the impact of social media on privacy and even democracy. This film’s advantage is that the speakers in The Social Dilemma include top executives from Twitter, Instagram, Pinterest, Facebook, and others. The experts assure us their intentions were good -- even the one whose job title at Facebook was head of “monetization”. Yet all are deeply concerned about what they’ve created, and one confesses that he worked all day on making his site irresistibly seductive and then found himself unable to resist the very algorithmic tricks he helped to create when he went home at night. The most important lesson from the film is that people should question everything they read online, especially if it is presented in a way that reflects a detailed understanding of personal inclinations and preferences. Viewers should learn to resist the “attention extraction model” that makes social media seem friendly and reinforcing. As the New York Times has advised, “Unplug and run”. After viewing The Social Dilemma, join the Diversity Film Series audience for Q & A discussion with Rebecca Wexler, Assistant Professor of Law at UC Berkeley Law, and Co-Director of the Berkeley Center for Law & Technology. Wexler teaches, researches, and writes on issues concerning data, technology, and criminal justice. Sign up at www.diversityfilmseries.org for the Diversity Film viewing on Thursday, May 13, from 5:00-6:00 p.m. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by the City of Piedmont, Piedmont League of Women Voters and Piedmont School District. articles.text: The prospect of a new concert tour lured me to Southern California. But the reward wasn’t musical. My sister, a former Deputy Attorney General, is a graduate of the CIA boot camp. But it’s not the CIA you are thinking about. This CIA is the Culinary Institute of America. They offer a wide range of classes and you can put your learning to good use immediately. During my recent visit, the first breakfast I had was one of my favorites – popovers. I told my sister that I had purchased readymade packages of popovers. She responded that popovers are so easy to make, you really don’t need a package. The basic recipe has a total of five ingredients – a cup of all-purpose flour, a little salt, 1 tablespoon of butter, a cup of milk and two eggs. That’s it. You can enjoy them as they come out of the oven or serve them with your favorite jam or fruit. The second memorable meal was a braised veal roast with carrots and boiled potatoes. My sister decided to splurge. She bought the veal roast from the kosher butcher. When she told me that the meat cost $70, I was a bit surprised. However, considering that the quality was much better than the meat from a supermarket, the cost was warranted. Another consideration was that it served eight people and the bones were enjoyed by the dog. Thus, the cost was less than $10 per person. The next memorable meal was actually rather easy. My sister prepared a basic crêpe mix which can be used to make a manicotti An elegant breakfast with delicious crêpes – very easy to make. at the same time as the veal roast.

articles.text: Piedmont author Kelly Corrigan released a children’s book, Hello World! on April 20. A New York Times bestselling author, Corrigan wrote this book in honor of her father and his endless enthusiasm. Hello World! celebrates the people in everyone’s life and the meaningful connections that come from asking each other questions. Hello World! reminds readers that the journeys we take through life are all about the people along the way. With her trademark inspirational messages, Corrigan’s book is for kids about to embark on new adventures. Illustrator Stacy Ebert brings the 44-page story to life with vivid artwork. The book is primarily for children age three to seven. The book is published by Flamingo Books and is available at bookstores. For more information, go to Kellycorrigan.com. Kelly Corrigan’s newest book is a story for children, Hello, World!

articles.text: Piedmont resident Shanti Brien published a new book on March 2, 2021 about criminal justice, titled Almost Innocent: From Searching to Saved in America’s Criminal Justice System. The book is her insider account as a lawyer of the messy, tragic, and often unjust legal system in America. From defunding the police to the college admissions scandal, from the national rise in crime to seditious mobs escaping prosecution, Brien tackles some of the most urgent criminal justice topics of today. Part memoir, part political commentary, Almost Innocent details the stories of nine legal cases. It goes behind the headlines to break down and challenge the dichotomies our country grapples with – us versus them, good versus bad, guilt versus innocence, and Black versus white. Weaving stories of the obviously guilty to the surprisingly innocent, the book is a love letter to the author’s clients. Though their profiles are as individual as their sentences – the teenage gang member whose gun never fired, the victim of the world’s most vindictive HOA, the soft-spoken three-strikes rapist, and the getaway driver – all touched Shanti Brien’s life in surprising ways. Almost Innocent is an intimate portrait of the criminal justice system, offering suggestions for how it can be more fair, more humane, and more just. “Almost Innocent” is published by Amplify Publishing, Ingram, Baker & Taylor, and American West. It is available at most bookstores and outlets. For more information go to www. ShantiBrien.com

articles.text: Tickets to exhibitions on sale now San Francisco’s Legion of Honor museum. The Legion of Honor, part of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, is re-opening with special member preview days beginning May 6. The Legion of Honor will require timed tickets for every visitor, including general admission to its current exhibition,” Tickets will be released in 60-day increments to ensure social distancing. Health guidelines have reduced the capacity at any one time to less than 25 percent of the museum’s capacity. Pompeii Exhibit The “Last Summer in Pompeii” exhibition examines the fiery eruption of Mount Vesuvius, which left Pompeii and nearby villages and farms buried under pumice and hot ash. “Pompeii” brings audiences back to this world prior to the devastation, with a focus on everyday life, culture, and the food and drink of Pompeii. Pots, pans, and other household items for the preparation and serving of food is displayed, as well as works of art that reveal the luxury of wealthy Romans who called the oasis home. To learn more about the exhibition, and to secure timed reservations, visit https://legionof honor.famsf.org/exhibitions/ pompeii. To learn about the extra safety precautions Legion of Honor is taking when re-opening, visit https://legionofhonor.famsf.org/ legion/visiting/museum-policies. Ongoing digital programs In addition, a new partnership between the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco (the de Young and Legion of Honor) and the “SeeBlackWomxn” collective has launched a five-part series focused on the contemporary Black Arts scene. The collective was founded by artists and activists Tahirah Rasheed, Angela Hennessy, Dana King, and Jamani Montague, and celebrates the lineage and legacy of Black women in contemporary arts. SeeBlackWomxn serves as a collective narrative of artists and writers who contribute to Black feminist theory. The platform emphasizes self-representation and aims to stray from the stereotypical tropes assigned to Black women and identifying women. The series is programmed through the museums’ “Virtual Wednesdays” and Local Voices podcast, which aims to explore the impact of public art on the Bay Area community. This year, notable artists who contributed to the podcast include Lava Thomas, Catherine Wagner, and Alison Saar, musical duo Mercury Soul, Fredrika Newton of the Dr. Huey P. Newton Foundation, the #SayHerName Movement, Susan Cervantes of the Precita Eyes Muralists, artist duo Rue Bainbridge, artist and composer Gryphon Rue, and artist Peter Simensky. Visit https://www.youtube. com/watch?v=Yk9TV4-GA78 to watch the conversation, and visit https://www.seeblackwomxn. com to learn more about the collective.
articles.title: Legion of Honor to reopen in May

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet will stream Helgi Tomasson’s Romeo & Juliet from May 6 through May 26. The multi-capture, cinematic production was performed at the San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House. It was SF Ballet’s last production prior to 2020 COVID-19 closures. It was last performed in 2019 at the Royal Danish Opera House in Copenhagen. The production premiered during SF Ballet’s 1994 Repertory season and is considered a signature work of the San Francisco Ballet company, which has performed it worldwide. Tomasson’s Romeo and Juliet is performed with music under the direction of Martin West. The production includes former principal dancers Maria Kochetkova and Davit Karapetyan in the title roles. Pascal Molat, now on faculty at SF Ballet School, is cast as Mercutio. The opulent set is designed by Jens-Jacob Worsaae, with lighting design by Thomas Skelton. This was Worsaae’s final collaboration with Tomasson before he died shortly after the ballet’s premiere. “I think it was the most beautiful work he’d ever done, and yet he did not see it. That’s one reason why this production is very, very special to me,” Tomasson said. To purchase tickets to the streaming production, visit https://www.sfballet.org/productions/digital-program-06/.
articles.title: SF Ballet to stream Romeo & Juliet beginning May 6

articles.text: A scene from Diablo Ballet’s production of Once Upon a Time. Tickets are now on sale for Diablo Ballet’s production of Once Upon a Time, which will premiere on May 7. The performance will be available on demand from Friday through Sunday, May 7-9, and the following weekend, May 14-16. Diablo Ballet, located in Walnut Creek, is an award-winning professional dance company founded in 1993. Dancers perform a collection of classical and contemporary works, and have performed throughout the United States, Europe, and South America. Once Upon a Time is the story of a young man who accidentally finds himself as the male lead in favorite classic fairytales like Cinderella, Snow White, Alice in Wonderland, and Little Red Riding Hood. The unconventional ballet relies on the age-old narrative of “happily-ever-after,” with the music of George Gershwin and Benjamin Britten, and choreography by Julia Adam. Purchasing a virtual ticket will allow you to view the performance either weekend. Ticket holders can watch the on-demand performance multiple times throughout that weekend. To purchase tickets call (925) 943-7467, or visit: https://diabloballet.org/ onceuponatime/.
articles.title: Diablo Ballet presents Once Upon A Time

articles.text: Concert will feature Alexander String Quartet Gold Coast Chamber Players’ season finale, “Dvorak’s America”, takes place this Saturday, May 1 at 7 p.m. “Dvorak’s America” explores the impact that Spirituals and Native American music had on Czech composer Antonin Dvorak during his time in America. The project, three years in the making, highlights the interconnectedness of these cultures. The program will feature the composer’s String Quintet, op. 97, and the Lento from his String Quartet op. 96, both of which are nicknamed “the American.” Original music by Mary Youngblood for Native American flute, “Within My Heart” and “Beneath the Raven Moon,” as well as her arrangement of “Amazing Grace”, represent what Dvorak heard during his stay in America. Dvorak proclaimed that African American Spirituals are “the heart of American music,” and the genre serves as perhaps the greatest Western influence on the composer. Spirituals that will be performed in this program include “Swing Low Sweet Chariot,” “By an’ By,” and “My Lord What a Morning.” ConcludAlexander String Quartet: Zakarias Grafilo and Frederick Lifsitz, violins, Sandy Wilson, cello and violist David Samuel, a recent addition. ing the program will be “Goin’ Home,” from the composer’s New World Symphony. Alexander String Quartet will lead the ensemble, marking one of the first performances with their new violist, David Samuel. Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast Players and a frequent collaborated with the Quartet, will join its members for “Dvorak’s America.” The event will be livestreamed via YouTube at 7 p.m. on Saturday, May 1. For more information and to obtain tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com, or call (925) 283-3728.
articles.title: Gold Coast hosts Dvorak program May 1

articles.text: Conductor Donato Cabrera Donato Cabrera will conduct the San Francisco Conservatory of Music Orchestra on Saturday, May 1 in a live-stream performance at 7:30 p.m. Cabrera is the current Music Director of the California Symphony as well as the Las Vegas Philharmonic. articles.text: Photos by Steve Goodall Tsavo (left), a male giraffe from Fresno Chaffee Zoo, enjoys a snack with female giraffe Kijiji at The Oakland Zoo’s African Savanna. The Oakland Zoo proudly announced that Tsavo, a fouryear-old male reticulated giraffe, arrived in Oakland from the Fresno Zoo on April 22. Earlier in the week another young male giraffe came to Oakland from San Diego Zoo. Oakland Zoo’s animal care team had been seeking compatible additions to the herd after suffering the loss of four giraffes to age in recent years. The need to cultivate a new herd comparable in number to those in the wild is critical to the social structure and well-being of giraffes. Giraffes are highly social animals that in the wild maintain relationships with many individuals. Tsavo’s presence will provide the giraffe herd at Oakland Zoo with a more robust and needed social structure, bringing the herd to a healthy six in number. “Animal welfare goes beyond the daily care and dedicated attention our animal residents receive from our animal care staff. Planning for their futures and strengthening their social structures also play a vital role in our animals’ lives,” explained newly named Oakland Zoo Director Nik Dehejia. Tsavo’s arrival follows months of planning between Fresno Zoo and Oakland Zoo. Before his departure, the animal care team at Fresno Chaffee Zoo used positive reinforcement training to help persuade him to complete new behaviors voluntarily which were needed for his transport, such as walking through specific areas of the giraffe night house. “We are excited for our newest giraffe additions to join our giraffe herd,” said Colleen Kinzley, VP of Animal Care at Oakland Zoo. “The diversity of ages and mixture of males and females in this herd will be similar to the social dynamics that giraffe experience in the wild. This addition reinforces the importance of animal welfare at the Zoo.” The young male giraffe from the San Diego Zoo is still unnamed. The zoo is currently having their Homeward Bound Silent Auction and one of the auction items is the right to name him. Over the past 15 years, giraffes in Africa have faced a “silent extinction” with a 40 percent decline in their population. Both the Oakland and Fresno zoos partner with the Reticulated Giraffe Project in Kenya, a conservation organization dedicated to working with local communities in Africa to help reduce human-wildlife conflict and habitat loss to preserve endangered giraffe populations in the wild. For more information, go to Oaklandzoo.org. Tsavo and a male adolescent giraffe from San Diego Zoo explore their new habitat at The Oakland Zoo.

Let’s consider some of them: • Your views on helping your family Your decisions about helping your family are clearly going to be a major part of your financial strategy – and this is true at virtually all stages of your life. When your children are young, you’ll need to decide if you’re going to put away money for their college education, and, if so, how much, and in what investment vehicles. When they’re young adults, you may also need to decide how much financial support you’re willing to provide for things such as the down payment on a new home. And when you’re drawing up your estate plans, you’ll need to consider how to distribute assets to your children, grandchildren or other family members. • Your personal beliefs As someone with civic, ethical and moral concerns, you want to positively affect the world around you. And that’s why you may feel compelled to make charitable gifts throughout your life and then make philanthropy part of your legacy. To accomplish these objectives, you’ll want to include gifting techniques in your financial strategy today and your estate plans for tomorrow. Of course, for the estate planning component, you’ll need to work with your tax and legal advisors. • Your purpose in life when you retire When you retire, you may be stepping off a career path, but you’re also entering a world of possibilities. How will you define, and live out, your new sense of purpose at this stage of your life? Do you seek to broaden your horizons by traveling around the world? Do you want to give back more to the community by volunteering? Can you spend more time pursuing the hobbies you enjoy? Each of these choices will carry different financial implications for how much you’ll need to accumulate for retirement and how much you will need to take out each year from your retirement accounts, such as your IRA and 401(k). • Your health Your physical and mental health can play big roles in your financial plans and outlook. On the most basic level, the healthier you are, and the better you take care of yourself, the lower your health care bills will likely be during retirement, which will affect the amount you need to put away for health care. And you also may need to prepare for the costs of long-term care, which can be enormous – in fact, a private room in a nursing home can easily cost $100,000 per year, according to the insurance company Genworth. It can be challenging to weave all these elements into a single, unified vision, so you may want to get some help from a financial professional. But, in any case, be prepared to look at your situation holistically – because, when putting together a lifetime’s financial strategy, every part of your life matters. articles.text: Tips on how to maximize your on-line shopping experience An antique Singer sewing machine is one of the many items that will be for sale starting May 1. This Saturday morning, May 1, set your alarms and check your internet connection, because the annual White Elephant Sale, held at Oakland Museum of California (OMCA), opens as an on-line shop at 8 a.m. sharp. This being OMCA’s first virtual event, a list of “pro-tips” have been provided by OMCA Woman’s Board volunteers, the group that organizes the event each year. These tips can also be found on the organization’s website by visiting https://www. whiteelephantsale.org/home/ pro-tips. ▪ You can “Shop By Department” or browse among the collections listed on our home page. Then you can browse page by page or narrow your choices by Category, Color, or Size. Or you can go straight to “Search” to find items that might be in one of several departments. ▪ Want to see some of our most wonderful, unusual, and odd things the sale is known for? Do a search for Vintage or Unique. ▪ If you think you’ll be shopping a few times during the sale, select a pickup date toward the end of May, so you can collect all your treasures in one trip. ▪ Plan to shop a few times during the sale. We’re not adding more items but there’s over 6000 items on hand. Keep looking: who knows what kind of treasures you’ll find! ▪ Do you really need to know if that dress has a belt, or if the badminton set comes with extra birdies? Sure, you can ask us, but someone else may snatch up the item before we can reply. Better to buy and hope for the best. ▪ Even after you put your items in your cart, it’s not yours until you pay for it. Keep in mind that someone else can still buy it before you have a chance to. ▪ This year, it’s really easy to buy complementary things across departments. Found a Thai table runner? Match it with that Thai terra cotta vase or a Thai cookbook. Found some nice jewelry? With one click you’ll find a jewelry box and a second click gets you a book on fine jewels. ▪ When you come to pick up your items, bring your mask. Bring bungee cords and ropes if you’re collecting large or bulky things. We can help with some heavy lifting but you will be the one to secure your items in your vehicle. ▪ Not sure if it will fit? Buy it. If you don’t like it, donate it to the 2022 White Elephant Sale. It all benefits the Oakland Museum of California. ▪ Everything is one of a kind. At these prices, there’s no wrong purchase. Caveat emptor Note that while you can shop from home, no shipping or delivery of items will be available. All items purchased must be picked up curbside at the warehouse, located at 333 Lancaster Street in Oakland. articles.text: Members of the Walking on Wednesday group stopped for a photo in Upper Dracena Park on April 21. Pictured are: Mark Greenberg (left), Andree Greenberg, Albert Chen, Nancy DeRoche and dog Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Kathy Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Jim Kao, and Bob Gustafson. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group assembled last Wednesday, April 21, for its second weekly walk of the year. After a year of no activity due to Covid-19, last week’s gathering was a “Goldilocks” walk in the park. A total of 22 people had registered for the walk, and ten were on hand for the day’s activity: Nancy DeRoche with her K-9 best friend Chili, Brenda Ferrero, Andree Greenberg, Mark Greenberg, Kathy Gustafson, Bob Gustafson, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Dick Carter, and first-time walker Albert Chen. Over the years Dracena Park has become one of Piedmont’s best recreational spots because of the City and Piedmont Beautification Foundation’s work and investment. This is an eight-acre park woven into the surrounding neighborhood. Its boundaries are Dracena, Blair, El Cerrito, Artuna Avenues and Park Way. It was a rock quarry in the early 20th century that supplied material for local streets and other construction. The area has been transformed since then into a beautiful park. The City recently reworked the park’s upper grass area. About two years ago the walkers were “sidewalk superintends” for the removal of a set of huge eucalyptus trees that threatened nearby homes. The walkers set off going down Magnolia Avenue past Piedmont High School, where they admired the new STEAM classroom building and the construction going on for the school’s new theater and offices. Some stories were told by walkers about the original, classically designed Piedmont High School that was built in 1921 and the buildings that replaced it in the 1970s, which were largely demolished recently in order to build the new structures. The group then went up Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue to Blair Avenue, and down Blair to Dracena Avenue, passing lovely homes and front yards along the way. Rhododendrons had started to explode with color and the beautiful white dogwood flowers were still in bloom. The walkers entered the park on Dracena Avenue at the large lawn at the top of the park, then down the dog path shaded by redwood trees past Storyteller Bridge that was rebuilt in 2014. They came to the popular children’s playground at the park’s base with its climbing wall, cement slide, and play structure. Kids were enjoying them and also chasing soap bubbles on the nearby lawn. The group walked the loop at the base of the former rock quarry, and emerged on Artuna Ricardo Avenue. They went up Ricardo to Arroyo Avenue, down to York Drive to Cambridge Way, and up to Latham, Piedmont’s only roadway with street in its name. The walkers went up Latham and noted a long, narrow home that was built in the 1950s on land created after the Key System train line closed and sold its right-of-way land for house development. The group crossed Oakland Avenue and went up to San Carlos Avenue, a split-level street, where they walked on both the upper and lower portion of the street. Rounding the corner onto el Cerrito Avenue, Dick Carter pointed out his childhood home and a classic Piedmont sycamore tree in front that has a noticeably wider trunk that the surrounding trees. Dick told the group this tree’s trunk is much larger than the others because his father watered the grass car strip in front of their home constantly during his over 50 years living there. The walkers went down El Cerrito to Magnolia Avenue and back up it to the Exedra with additional personal and local history stories being told along the way. The 90-minute, three-mile walk made for a “Goldilocks” morning with a beautiful park, great streets, sites, stories, and friends. Everyone agreed it had been just right. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge, and new walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required. Sign up at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or contact John Wilk at the Piedmont Recreation Department (jwilk@piedmont.ca.gov) for more information. Paris, our world-famous city, is certainly emotionally displaced by the coronavirus and has been economically pushed into extraordinary hibernation. Yet, people are hopeful. Despite the pandemic, Parisians still complain often and seriously about the chilly, rainy weather and gray skies that seem to plague every otherwise nice day. To escape the chill and the Paris lockdown, the fortunate are headed to their country places or to the south of France, especially Nice and Aix-Provence. Such is the irony that the coronavirus weather is balmy and sunny with a forecast of the temperature reaching the mid-70s most days this week. Gazing from our open windows, lovely as that is, we literally have no place to go. The Piedmont Police Department’s speed trailer, parked in front of the station, was festooned with bright spring flowers. On the back was an orange umbrella shaped like a flower flanked by tall branches of pink dogwood and lime-green viburnum. The day before, Kang and McAuliffe journeyed to the San Francisco Flower Market at 5 a.m. to prepare for their flower pop-up. Kang explained that the project was inspired by New Yorkbased florist Lewis Miller, who started the “Flower Flash” craze. “A ‘flash’ is exactly that: an unexpected burst of colorful flowers in the most unexpected places, and for a short period of time,” Kang said. “You will see [Lewis’] amazing flower flashes in street garbage cans, construction sites, chain link fences, phone booths, hot dog carts, and bus stops. My favorites are the ones with flowers set against walls covered with graffiti. What I find so appealing, as a former New Yorker, is his guerrilla-style street art using the city’s grit, grime and graffiti as props for his flashes,” Kang said. “This year I saw the speed trailer parked in front of the police station and thought, why not? I wrote to Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, who approved our project and assigned Capt. Chris Monahan to assist us,” Kang explained. Kang and McAuliffe asked Monahan if he could change the speed trailer’s electronic sign to show the message, “April Showers Bring May...” The pair thought it would be clever to omit the word “flowers,” because the trailer would be fashioned with a big arrangement of them. Staff photos “Chris [Monahan] was less sure, thinking that he would be getting calls from residents complaining that the message was incomplete,” she said. As the two stood near the newly decorated speed trailer, they were greeted with car-honks and passerby-shouts of approval. The finishing touches were put on just as the sun rose that morning. “The smiles and positive comments that we received made the whole project worthwhile,” Kang said.

articles.text: Piedmont officers observed a white Chevrolet Malibu fail to stop at a stop sign at Wildwood and Nova on Monday morning, April 19. A records check revealed that the vehicle had been stolen out of Hayward. The male driver was detained on scene, but he refused to provide his name. A records check identified him as Anthony White, 29, who was on probation for Domestic Violence and was listed as a possible suspect in the theft of the car. White was arrested for possession of a stolen vehicle and probation violations. He was transported to Santa Rita jail, but was refused at the jail for a medical reason and was transported to John George psychiatric hospital in San Leandro. White was later released from the hospital after being issued a citation and a notice to appear in court.

articles.text: Piedmont Police officers were alerted that two stolen vehicles had entered the city on Tuesday afternoon, April 20. Officers found a 2007 white Chevy Trailblazer stolen from San Francisco towing a stolen 1997 silver GMC Sonoma with a rope at Olive and Oakland Avenues. Officers conducted a “high risk” stop at Fairview and Grand Ave. When the suspects spotted the police, the person in the vehicle being towed jumped out of the SUV and into the GMC and the suspect fled at high speed. Officers recovered the Chevy Trailblazer and had it towed. The vehicle was missing the front license plate and its interior had been stripped.
